posts.title: Talking with your teenager about acne
posts.excerpt: Acne is common and treatable; the first visit is mostly a conversation.
posts.content:
Acne can affect confidence long before it affects the skin much. At the first visit we listen to the teenager first, look at the skin and agree one simple routine.

We review it after a few weeks, because most acne plans need time before anything changes.

posts.title: Choosing and using sunscreen
posts.excerpt: A plain guide to the amount, the timing and the shade and hat that go with it.
posts.content:
The best sunscreen is the one you will actually wear. Apply it generously to dry skin before going outside, and again after swimming or long hours outdoors.

Shade, a hat and sensible timing do as much as any cream.

posts.title: What a cosmetic consultation involves
posts.excerpt: The consultation comes first, is credited to treatment, and starts with your questions.
posts.content:
A cosmetic consultation is a conversation. Dr. Raman asks what bothers you, examines the skin and explains what treatments can and cannot do.

The $60 consultation fee is credited toward any treatment you choose.

posts.title: Eczema at home: a calm routine
posts.excerpt: A plain routine, applied every day, does more than any single product.
posts.content:
Eczema settles best with a routine that is boring and daily. Bathe briefly in lukewarm water, pat the skin dry and apply a plain, fragrance-free moisturiser within a few minutes, while the skin is still slightly damp.

Use a prescribed anti-inflammatory cream only on the patches it was given for, for as long as the doctor said, then go back to moisturiser alone. If the skin is weeping, very sore or not improving after two weeks, book a review.

posts.title: How often should you have a skin check?
posts.excerpt: For many adults once a year is enough; some need a closer schedule.
posts.content:
There is no single answer. Adults with few moles and no family history of melanoma may only need a check when something changes. People with many moles, fair skin, a history of sunburn or a close relative with melanoma are usually advised to come once a year.

Between visits, look at your own skin monthly in good light and ask someone to check your back. Call us about any spot that grows, bleeds, itches or changes colour.

posts.title: Your child's first dermatology visit
posts.excerpt: What to bring, what we ask, and how we keep the visit calm.
posts.content:
Bring a list of any creams you have used, and a photo if the rash comes and goes. Tell your child that the doctor is going to look at their skin and that nothing will hurt.

Dr. Castellano talks to the child first, looks at the skin in good light and explains the plan to both of you. You leave with it written down.
